title: Ketoacidosis in Paediatrics
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Ketoacidosis is an emergency characterised by high anion‑gap metabolic acidosis, ketonuria and hyperglycaemia or hypoglycaemia. Rapid recognition, fluid resuscitation and insulin (or bicarbonate in severe acidosis) are life‑saving.

sections.p: Ketoacidosis is defined by an anion‑gap metabolic acidosis (AG>12) with ketonuria/ketonemia and either hyperglycaemia (>250 mg/dL) or hypoglycaemia. In children, the classic picture is diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

t.b: Low pH and low HCO3 confirm metabolic acidosis
Hyperglycaemia >250 mg/dL suggests DKA; normal or low glucose points to other causes

sections.p: Severity is staged by pH and bicarbonate. In low‑resource settings, clinical signs (Kussmaul breathing, altered consciousness) guide urgency.

t.b: Kussmaul respirations and lethargy indicate severe acidosis

sections.p: In East Africa, the leading causes are type 1 diabetes, infections (UTI, pneumonia), and malnutrition. Alcoholic and euglycaemic ketoacidosis are rarer but important.
b: Type 1 diabetes onset or missed insulin

t.b: Positive ketones with high glucose = DKA; ketones with normal glucose = other ketoacidosis

sections.p: Children present with polyuria, polydipsia, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration and Kussmaul breathing. Severe cases show altered mental status and shock.

t.b: Dehydration and tachycardia indicate volume loss; fruity breath suggests ketones

sections.p: Basic labs are essential. When unavailable, clinical judgment and simple bedside tests guide management.

t.b: Hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia are common; correct before insulin
High glucose confirms DKA; low glucose rules out DKA

sections.p: Complications include cerebral oedema, hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, arrhythmias and sepsis. Early recognition prevents mortality.

t.b: Any new neurological deficit warrants imaging

sections.p: Treat the precipitating cause, correct dehydration with isotonic saline, start insulin, and monitor electrolytes. Bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidosis.
b: Insulin – continuous infusion after initial fluid bolus
Bicarbonate – if pH<7.0 or severe cerebral oedema

t.b: Avoid high doses to prevent hypoglycaemia
Give before insulin if K<5.5 mEq/L

sections.p: After stabilization, educate families on insulin adherence, infection control and regular glucose monitoring. Screen siblings for diabetes.
Other causes of metabolic acidosis such as lactic acidosis, renal tubular acidosis and sepsis can mimic ketoacidosis.
b: Lactic acidosis – AG>12 but no ketones
Renal tubular acidosis – normal glucose, no ketones
Sepsis – AG>12, may have ketones if malnourished

sections.p: Urine ketone strips may miss β‑hydroxybutyrate; serum bicarbonate can be normal early. Clinical context is essential.
b: Urine dipstick – negative in early ketosis
Serum bicarbonate – may be >15 mEq/L in mild DKA

t.b: Positive confirms ketosis even if urine negative

faq.q: What is the first step in managing a child with suspected DKA?
faq.a: Start isotonic saline for volume resuscitation before insulin.

faq.q: Why is potassium replaced before insulin?
faq.a: Insulin drives potassium into cells, risking hypokalaemia and arrhythmias.
Only if pH<7.0 or severe cerebral oedema; otherwise it is avoided.

exam: A 10‑year‑old presents with vomiting, abdominal pain and fruity breath. What is the most urgent investigation? — Arterial blood gas to confirm acidosis and guide treatment.
A child with DKA has a serum potassium of 3.2 mEq/L. What is the next step? — Replace potassium before starting insulin infusion.
A 7‑year‑old with DKA has a pH of 7.08. What adjunctive therapy is indicated? — Bicarbonate infusion only if pH<7.0 and no contraindication.
A patient with suspected ketoacidosis has normal glucose but positive ketones. Which diagnosis is most likely? — Alcoholic or euglycaemic ketoacidosis.
During DKA management, the child develops seizures. What complication should you suspect? — Cerebral oedema.
A child with DKA is improving but develops hypoglycaemia. What is the cause? — Insulin driving glucose into cells and increased hepatic glucose utilisation.
A 12‑year‑old with DKA has a serum bicarbonate of 12 mEq/L. What is the severity stage? — Moderate ketoacidosis (pH 7.15‑7.24, HCO3 10‑14).
